name: Campus Cotton
audience: A student buying an everyday white tee online
goal: Choose a size and understand the total without hunting for information.
concern: Will it fit, and what will I actually pay?
other: A student using one plain tee as the starting point for creative outfits
otherneed: Styling ideas and clear product facts without adding a printed design
choice: Choose the straightforward single-purchase situation; fit and total are achievable needs to address. The creative-styling direction remains an untested alternative.
positionB: An unprinted white tee as a creative wardrobe starting point
a: Shop first: price, measurements, and size selection appear together.
b: Product context first: imagery and product facts lead into the same measurements and checkout.
why: The selected shopper can get to fit and price information immediately.
sources: Put measurements next to size selection.
Product options and membership pricing paths
Explain the single-item offer without extra pricing paths.
Use specific product facts rather than vague premium claims.
story1: As a shopper unsure about fit, I want garment measurements beside sizes so I can choose with more confidence.
feature1: An expandable measurement guide beside a required size selector.
check1: Open the guide, return to the selector, and keep the selected size.
story2: As a price-conscious shopper, I want an itemized total so I can understand the demo purchase.
feature2: Quantity control and a summary using one $25 classroom concept price.
check2: Two shirts show $50; demo shipping and tax are explicitly $0.
story3: As a shopper, I want a clear confirmation so I know the simulated checkout completed.
feature3: Validated checkout followed by a demo reference and stored order.
check3: Missing size/email prevents checkout; a valid submission produces a reference.
defer: Discount codes, accounts, bulk orders, and real payments.
task: Find the measurement guide, choose M, add two shirts, and complete a simulated checkout.
feedback: I found the size options but did not notice where measurements were.
change: Place the measurement disclosure immediately above the size selector in both versions.
retest: Ask the reviewer to locate the guide without a hint and repeat the task.
limit: AI-generated shirt imagery is a concept, not a photograph of manufactured stock. Fabric, measurements, and policies are classroom assumptions.

brand.support: One everyday white tee. Check the measurements, choose your size, and see the whole demo total before you decide.
brand.promise: A straightforward single-tee purchase with fit and total visible.
brand.niche: A commuter buying one everyday tee without navigating bundle or membership offers.
tips: Lay a tee you already like flat.
Compare chest width and length with the labeled centimeter guide.
Check quantity and the itemized demo total before submitting.
brand.trace: R1 shows fit/length information; R2 offers several purchasing paths. I chose a direct voice and a nearby measurement guide to support one uncomplicated purchase. This need is still a hypothesis.
brand.limit: The clarity idea is supported by page observations, not evidence that a student market prefers our offer.

persuasion.element: Before you choose a size — a free preparation guide
persuasion.mechanism: Offer useful guidance before asking the visitor to choose or request.
persuasion.limit: The page offers value; no change in purchase or request rates was measured.

persuasion.element: Welcoming language that addresses the visitor’s situation
persuasion.mechanism: A sincere relatable voice may make the offer feel approachable.
persuasion.limit: We have not measured this effect; no invented customers or testimonials are used.

name: Studio White
tag: One white tee. A considered choice.
audience: An early-career creative choosing a simple workday wardrobe
goal: Understand the fit and product details before choosing one tee.
concern: Does the presentation explain a meaningful difference?
other: A shopper seeking the lowest available price
otherneed: Rapid price comparison and frequent discounts
choice: Choose the workday shopper. Specific information and a restrained presentation fit this concept better than price-led promotions.
a: Editorial first: product story and material concept precede the purchase panel.
b: Product facts first: fit, price, and selection lead; the story follows.
why: Product details are accessible immediately while the visual style still supports the brand.
sources: Use specific product facts rather than vague premium claims.
Professional-use context and flat/worn product photos
Show an honest use case; do not invent performance or provenance claims.
Put measurements next to size selection.
story1: As a workday shopper, I want fit measurements before buying so I can judge the silhouette.
feature1: Labeled flat-garment measurements and a size selector.
check1: The guide labels centimeters and distinguishes garment dimensions from body measurements.
story2: As a careful buyer, I want a clear material description so I can understand the concept.
feature2: A visible product-facts section with classroom assumptions labeled.
check2: A visitor can locate material, fit, and care without opening checkout.
story3: As a buyer, I want to review my choices before completing the demo order.
feature3: An editable quantity, size, and total before validated confirmation.
check3: Three shirts show $126; confirmation states that no real order or payment occurred.
defer: Subscriptions, performance claims, provenance certification, and real fulfillment.
task: Find the product facts, choose L, review three shirts, and complete the demo checkout.
feedback: The story was attractive, but I had to search for practical product details.
change: Choose the facts-first version and keep a labeled product-facts section beside the purchase controls.
retest: Ask a peer to find fit and material information before selecting a size.
limit: No manufacturing or sustainability claim is verified. Concept price $42 is an assumption, not a market-tested price.

brand.support: A plain white starting point for your workday wardrobe. Explore the fit and classroom product details, then choose what works for you.
brand.promise: A considered starting point for a creative workday wardrobe.
brand.niche: An early-career creative assembling a simple workday outfit.
tips: Compare the flat measurements with a tee you already own.
Think about the layer you would wear over a plain white tee.
Read the concept product facts before deciding on size and quantity.
brand.trace: Buck Mason uses specific production context, and Cuts presents a workday use case. I chose a calm Creator voice because I like that look. I have not yet shown that this audience values the same emphasis.
brand.limit: The concept price is not validated, and polished imagery does not establish better materials or manufacturing.

name: Room Ready
tag: A clearer first step for furniture assembly.
audience: A first-apartment Newark-area renter who needs help assembling a desk
goal: Describe the item and request help without assuming a booking is confirmed.
concern: What information is needed, and what happens after I submit?
other: An experienced renter replacing a small shelving unit
otherneed: A quick way to describe a familiar assembly job and understand follow-up
choice: Serve the renter first, with a small request summary to demonstrate the handoff to the operator.
positionA: First-apartment assembly requests with extra guidance
positionB: Quick repeat assembly inquiries for experienced renters
a: Service first: explain scope and next steps before the request form.
b: Request first: show the short form immediately, with scope and process alongside it.
why: The scope and confirmation language are clearer before the visitor starts the form.
sources: Task, location, provider comparison, then confirmation
Explain the steps before the request.
The live assembly page sends new customers to Angi; Handy web booking is no longer available
Explain the handoff honestly and verify the live page rather than relying on older search summaries.
Assembly offered through Taskrabbit with follow-up steps
Distinguish a request from a confirmed appointment; this is a partner channel, not an independent competitor.
story1: As a renter, I want to know what assembly work is supported so I can decide whether to inquire.
feature1: A short scope statement: desks, chairs, and shelving; no electrical, mounting, or repair work.
check1: The supported work and exclusions are visible before submitting.
story2: As a renter, I want to provide my item and preferred window so the operator can assess the request.
feature2: Required service, preferred window, and demo-email fields.
check2: An empty required field prevents submission and a valid request retains the selected values.
story3: As an operator, I want a complete request summary so I can identify the next action.
feature3: A receipt/reference and a same-session request history.
check3: The receipt says request received, not appointment confirmed, and the record appears in history.
defer: Provider matching, real addresses, payments, live availability, and automated quotes.
task: Request assembly for a desk, select a preferred window, and explain whether you have a confirmed appointment.
feedback: The original button sounded like an instant confirmed booking.
change: Use “Send demo request” and explain that an operator would confirm scope, price, and availability later.
retest: Ask the reviewer whether the receipt guarantees an appointment; they should answer no.
limit: No actual service, operator notification, or scheduling integration exists. Any price shown is illustrative.

brand.support: Moving into your first place? Tell us what needs assembling and when you prefer help. A request starts the conversation; it does not reserve a time.
brand.promise: A helpful first step for renters unfamiliar with assembly requests.
brand.niche: A first-apartment renter who needs help describing a desk assembly job.
tips: Identify whether the item is a desk, chair, or shelving.
If this were a real request, keep the product instructions handy.
Choose a preferred window; an operator would discuss scope, price, and availability later.
brand.trace: Taskrabbit explains steps and IKEA names the service handoff. We chose a Caregiver voice, a preparation list, and explicit pending language so a first-time renter knows what to do next.
brand.limit: No service competence, insurance, provider checks, or live availability has been established.

name: Study Slot
tag: Tell us the topic. Choose a time to ask for help.
audience: A first-year student requesting help with introductory web development
goal: Describe a topic and request a suitable tutoring window.
concern: Will the tutor know what I need, and is the time actually available?
other: A student preparing a broad web-development interview review
otherneed: A way to identify many topics and compare tutor expertise
choice: Design for the student’s request while including the information the tutor needs to respond.
a: Topic first: explain supported topics, then collect the request.
b: Time first: show the request controls first and list topics alongside them.
why: Topic context helps a student decide whether this service fits their question before choosing a time.
sources: Booking and client-management features; education use cases
Collect the topic before the session.
Subject-specific tutor listings, qualifications, and displayed reviews
Compare a real tutoring alternative with our narrow beginner request concept.
story1: As a student, I want to see supported topics so I can decide whether to request help.
feature1: HTML, CSS, and introductory JavaScript listed with boundaries.
check1: The site makes clear it offers guidance, not completion of assessed work.
story2: As a student, I want to choose a topic and preferred window so I can make a useful request.
feature2: Labeled topic/window controls and validated demo email.
check2: Submission requires both choices; selecting a preference does not claim live availability.
story3: As a tutor, I want the request details together so I can prepare and respond.
feature3: Pending-request confirmation and readable request history.
check3: The receipt includes topic, preferred window, and pending status; no calendar event is claimed.
defer: Live calendar sync, accounts, AI tutoring, real notifications, and payments.
task: Request help with CSS for a preferred window and explain the next step.
feedback: I thought selecting a time reserved it immediately.
change: Label it “Preferred window” and show “Pending tutor confirmation” in the receipt.
retest: Ask the reviewer to explain the difference between requesting a window and booking a confirmed session.
limit: No tutor is contacted. Availability is fictional; this is a request workflow, not a live booking platform.

brand.support: Stuck on HTML, CSS, or a first JavaScript question? Start with the topic and a preferred window. A tutor would confirm the next step.
brand.promise: An approachable first request for beginner web-development guidance.
brand.niche: A first-year student who can name a topic but is unsure how to ask for help.
tips: Pick HTML, CSS, or introductory JavaScript.
Write down what you expected and what happened instead.
Bring your own attempt; support means understanding the work, not having it completed for you.
brand.trace: Wyzant shows subject-specific tutor choices; Calendly and Acuity show scheduling workflows. I chose a patient Sage voice and a preparation list. I have not connected each persona need to a specific observation or checked whether beginners prefer this narrower offer.
brand.limit: The references do not prove tutoring demand, tutor competence, or that the preferred window is available.

name: Maya Chen
audience: A recruiter scanning for an early-career web-development intern
goal: Find two projects and understand the student’s actual contribution.
concern: Can I distinguish a course exercise from professional experience?
other: A local small-business owner considering a student collaborator
otherneed: Clear examples of useful customer-facing work and contact information
choice: Prioritize the internship recruiter; keep explanations readable for a nontechnical visitor too.
positionB: Customer-facing work for local small-business collaborators
a: Projects first: two case-study cards lead into résumé and profiles.
b: About first: learning goals and personal brand lead into the same project evidence.
why: A recruiter can reach the work and the individual contribution in fewer steps.
sources: Role introduction, project/experience evidence, professional links
Make role and evidence easy to find.
An article-led site that demonstrates teaching
Use a short explanation to show reasoning.
A concise introduction and writing links
Keep the introduction brief. These are experienced practitioners, not student achievement benchmarks.
story1: As a recruiter, I want to find two projects quickly so I can inspect relevant work.
feature1: Two project cards linked to case-study details and runnable examples.
check1: Both projects are labeled course projects and their demo links open the correct examples.
story2: As a reviewer, I want individual contribution details so I can understand what the student did.
feature2: Case studies distinguish individual work from team outcomes.
check2: The group case study names one personally owned feature and one peer-review task.
story3: As a recruiter, I want résumé and profile information so I can continue reviewing the student.
feature3: Readable résumé, sample GitHub README, and LinkedIn example content.
check3: Profile links open readable, clearly labeled fictional examples; a real student uses actual account links.
defer: Blog platform, elaborate animation, analytics, and invented testimonials.
task: Find the T-shirt project, identify the student’s group contribution, and locate the résumé.
feedback: The group card explained the product but not what Maya personally built.
change: Add a “My contribution” paragraph to the group case study and a direct résumé navigation link.
retest: Ask the reviewer to name Maya’s contribution and find the résumé without hints.
limit: Maya is a fictional student. The profile examples, résumé, and contribution statements model a submission; they are not a real person’s credentials.

brand.support: I’m an NJIT student practicing web development with AI. Explore two course projects, the choices behind them, and the parts I designed, built, and checked.
brand.promise: Make my actual student work and contribution easy to inspect.
brand.niche: An internship recruiter looking for concrete early-career project evidence.
tips: Begin with a person and one task, not a long feature list.
Write what success would look like before asking AI to build.
Try the task with a peer, make a change, and check again.
brand.trace: Brittany Chiang puts role and work evidence together; Josh Comeau demonstrates thinking through explanation. I chose a Creator voice that points to decisions and artifacts rather than claiming expertise.
brand.limit: Course work is evidence of practice, not professional employment, a hiring result, or proof of advanced expertise.

persuasion.element: Linked course projects and individual contribution notes
persuasion.mechanism: Relevant inspectable work can demonstrate competence without claiming senior credentials.
persuasion.limit: This is student practice, not professional employment or a hiring outcome.

name: Jordan Rivera
audience: A team lead assessing a student’s problem-solving and collaboration
goal: Understand one business decision and the student’s own implementation and QA work.
concern: Is there evidence behind the claims, including AI-assisted work?
other: A recruiter quickly checking minimum project and contact information
otherneed: A concise summary, projects, résumé, and professional links
choice: Prioritize clear project reasoning while retaining easy access to résumé and profiles.
positionA: Decision evidence for a technical team lead
positionB: A concise overview for an internship recruiter
a: Evidence first: a short decision and its validation introduce the projects.
b: Introduction first: role direction and skills precede project evidence.
why: The selected audience can inspect a concrete decision instead of relying on a list of tools.
sources: Role introduction, project/experience evidence, professional links
Make role and evidence easy to find.
An article-led site that demonstrates teaching
Use a short explanation to show reasoning.
A concise introduction and writing links
Keep the introduction brief. These are experienced practitioners, not student achievement benchmarks.
story1: As a team lead, I want a concise case study so I can assess the student’s reasoning.
feature1: Problem, alternatives, choice, feedback, and limitation in each case study.
check1: A visitor can identify one decision and its reason in each project.
story2: As a reviewer, I want to see how AI output was checked so I can assess ownership.
feature2: A short AI-use and verification statement tied to a feature.
check2: The statement describes a specific human check and does not claim unrun tests passed.
story3: As a recruiter, I want clear profile and résumé access so I can evaluate next steps.
feature3: Dedicated professional-presence section and résumé download.
check3: Profile links open readable, clearly labeled fictional examples; a real student uses actual account links.
defer: Automated skills scores, advanced dashboard, and unsupported FDE-readiness claims.
task: Find a research-driven decision, explain Jordan’s group contribution, and locate the professional profiles.
feedback: I saw tools listed, but I could not tell how Jordan checked AI-generated work.
change: Add an AI-use and verification paragraph to each case study.
retest: Ask the reviewer to explain one check Jordan performed and identify a limitation.
limit: Jordan is fictional. This is a model of an introductory student portfolio, not evidence of employment or internship eligibility.

brand.support: I’m an NJIT student learning to make useful web workflows. My course projects show the problem, my contribution, and what I checked after using AI.
brand.promise: Explain the decisions and checks behind a small working project.
brand.niche: A technical team lead assessing a student’s reasoning and collaboration.
tips: Name the input you want to test.
Write the expected result before trying it.
Record what happened, including limits or failures.
brand.trace: Lee Robinson keeps introductions brief and links writing; Josh Comeau explains technical ideas. I chose a Sage voice, but I still describe both managers and recruiters without prioritizing a reader task.
brand.limit: Listing a check is weaker than explaining its input, expected result, and actual outcome.
